narrative: The Philosophy major consists of a total of at least 48 units in Philosophy, at least 36 of which must be upper-division. Students must follow the requirements of one of the two concentrations: Core Philosophy and Ethics and Public Policy. For details, consult the Philosophy Department.

MAJOR REGULATIONS
PREREQUISITES.............................................. Check the General Catalog for the prerequisites to all listed courses.
P/NP GRADING OPTION................................. Not allowed for any course applied to the major (prep or UD), including courses applied to the major from other departments.
SUBSTITUTIONS.............................................. In the major requirements permissible only by petition to the department chair and dean.
G.P.A REQUIREMENTS.................................. At least 2.0 overall UC average in all upper-division major courses and all courses (Prep and UD) for the major.
DOUBLE MAJORS............................................ With the approval of each department chairperson, up to a total of 8 units may be applied simultaneously to both UD majors.

nodes.title: Short Introduction to Philosophy
groups: Preparation for the Major: Up to three lower-division courses in Philosophy
nodes.description: An introductory course in western philosophy.

nodes.title: Critical Thinking
groups: Preparation for the Major: Up to three lower-division courses in Philosophy
nodes.description: Practical reasoning, argumentation, and the analysis of language as instruments of sound thinking in everyday life.

nodes.title: Introduction to Ethics
groups: Preparation for the Major: Up to three lower-division courses in Philosophy
nodes.description: An examination, at an introductory level, of such ethical issues as: why bemoral, moral relativism, the nature of virtues and vices; and possibly consideration of practical ethical problems such as abortion or war.

nodes.title: Biomedical Ethics
groups: Preparation for the Major: Up to three lower-division courses in Philosophy
nodes.description: An examination of philosophical thinking about moral issues raised by the practice of medicine. Traditional ethical theories and problems will serve as background to, and in turn be illuminated by, such issues as informed consent, paternalism, abortion, euthanasia, and genetic engineering.

nodes.title: History of Philosophy
groups: Preparation for the Major: Up to three lower-division courses in Philosophy
nodes.description: From Thales to Aristotle.

nodes.title: History of Philosophy
groups: Preparation for the Major: Up to three lower-division courses in Philosophy
nodes.description: From Medievals to Rationalists.

nodes.title: History of Philosophy
groups: Preparation for the Major: Up to three lower-division courses in Philosophy
nodes.description: From the Empiricists to Kant.

nodes.title: Ethics
groups: Concentration I - Core Philosophy: B.
Concentration I - Core Philosophy: D.
Concentration II - Ethics and Public Policy: B.
Concentration II - Ethics and Public Policy: E.
nodes.prereq_text: One prior course in philosophy; or, Philosphy 3 (may be taken concurrently)
nodes.description: An examination of the fundamental concepts, theories, and problems of moral or political philosophy.

nodes.title: Theory of Knowledge
groups: Concentration I - Core Philosophy: B.
Concentration I - Core Philosophy: D.
Concentration II - Ethics and Public Policy: C.
Concentration II - Ethics and Public Policy: E.
nodes.prereq_text: One prior course in philosophy.
nodes.description: Investigates fundamental questions surrounding the nature of human knowledge and human justification, such as: What do I know? What am I justified in believing? What is it to know something? What is it to hold a justified belief?

nodes.title: Philosophy of Language
groups: Concentration I - Core Philosophy: B.
Concentration I - Core Philosophy: D.
Concentration II - Ethics and Public Policy: C.
Concentration II - Ethics and Public Policy: E.
nodes.prereq_text: One prior course in philosophy.
nodes.description: Introduction to philosophical problems and theories concerning the nature of language. Topics typically include the notion of linguistic structure, theories of meaning and reference, names and descriptions, the relations between languages and thought, necessity and analytic truty, and conversational norms.

nodes.title: Philosophy of Mind
groups: Concentration I - Core Philosophy: B.
Concentration I - Core Philosophy: D.
Concentration II - Ethics and Public Policy: C.
Concentration II - Ethics and Public Policy: E.
nodes.prereq_text: One prior course in philosophy.
nodes.description: Discussion of some central questions about the mind: are people identical to their bodies? What is it to feel, believe, or desire something? What distinguishes intelligent thinking from a computer's activities? What is the connection between language and thought?

nodes.title: Metaphysics
groups: Concentration I - Core Philosophy: B.
Concentration I - Core Philosophy: D.
Concentration II - Ethics and Public Policy: C.
Concentration II - Ethics and Public Policy: E.
nodes.prereq_text: One prior course in philosophy.
nodes.description: Introduction to the philosophical study of the most general and fundamental features of reality. Topics vary, but may include universals, particulars, identity and individuation, substance, the nature of persons, causation, and the nature of time.

nodes.title: Introduction to the Philosophy of Science
groups: Concentration I - Core Philosophy: B.
Concentration I - Core Philosophy: D.
Concentration II - Ethics and Public Policy: C.
Concentration II - Ethics and Public Policy: E.
nodes.prereq_text: One prior course in philosophy; or major in physics, chemistry, or biology.
nodes.description: An introduction to the philosophical analysis of the concepts and methods of science, treating such topics as: explanation, confirmation, causation, scientific laws, the interpretation, meaning and reference of scientific theories, theory reduction and theory change, and scientific revolutions.

groups: Concentration II - Ethics and Public Policy: D.

nodes.title: Meaning and Reference
groups: Concentration I - Core Philosophy: B.
Concentration I - Core Philosophy: D.
Concentration II - Ethics and Public Policy: C.
Concentration II - Ethics and Public Policy: E.
nodes.prereq_text: Philosophy 183 (may be taken concurrently).
nodes.description: An examination of the classical theories of meaning and reference: John Stuart Mill, Gottlob Frege, Bertrand Russell, and the theory of direct reference. Investigation of solutions to the classical puzzles of meaning and reference.

nodes.title: Philosophy of Computing and Artificial Intelligence
groups: Concentration I - Core Philosophy: D.
Concentration II - Ethics and Public Policy: E.
nodes.prereq_text: A course from PHIL 100A-F, or two prior courses in philosophy.
nodes.description: Advances in artificial intelligence and the widespread use of computers in society confront us with many interesting philosophical questions. What is computation? Is AI really intelligence? Could computers ever think or feel? Is the Turing test a good test? Are we really computers? Are there decisions computers should never make? Do computers threaten our privacy in special ways? Should AI be regulated, and how? We will survey some of the controversies and puzzles that AI has provoked.

nodes.title: Political Philosophy
groups: Concentration I - Core Philosophy: D.
Concentration II - Ethics and Public Policy: D.
Concentration II - Ethics and Public Policy: E.
nodes.prereq_text: Major in philosophy, law & society, political science, or global and international studies.
nodes.description: Analysis of fundamental political conceptions; the state, sovereignty, political obligation, natural rights, natural law, etc.

groups: Concentration II - Ethics and Public Policy: D.

nodes.title: Philosophy of Science
groups: Concentration I - Core Philosophy: D.
Concentration II - Ethics and Public Policy: E.
nodes.prereq_text: A prior course in philosophy.
nodes.description: What is science? How does it differ from non-science? Course examines both the history of science and the history of philosophy of science in an effort to discover just what science is and what it has to offer.

nodes.title: Philosophy of Space and Time
groups: Concentration I - Core Philosophy: D.
Concentration II - Ethics and Public Policy: E.
nodes.prereq_text: A prior course in philosophy.
nodes.description: Is space a thing or a series of relations holding between objects? Does time pass differently for different observers, or in different parts of the universe? Consideration of these and other questions lead to an examination of contemporary physics.

nodes.title: Philosophy of Biology
groups: Concentration I - Core Philosophy: D.
Concentration II - Ethics and Public Policy: E.
nodes.prereq_text: A prior course in philosophy.
nodes.description: The biological sciences are distinctively different from the physical sciences. This course will focus on philosophical topics central to biology, such as evolutionary theory and its implications, the proper understanding of concepts such as function, fitness, selection, gene, or the nature of organisms and species.

nodes.title: Philosophical Foundations of Cognitive Science
groups: Concentration I - Core Philosophy: D.
Concentration II - Ethics and Public Policy: E.
nodes.prereq_text: A prior course in philosophy.
nodes.description: What is the mind and how can we model it? Cognitive science offers a distinctive approach to fundamental philosophical questions about the mind. This course begins with the classical foundations of cognitive science and surveys recent developments in the field, including neural networks, theories of embodiment, dynamical systems, and recent statistical approaches to cognition and artificial intelligence.

nodes.title: Philosophy and Neuroscience
groups: Concentration I - Core Philosophy: D.
Concentration II - Ethics and Public Policy: E.
nodes.prereq_text: A prior course in philosophy.
nodes.description: The brain is the seat of who we are. This course will focus on topics at the intersection of philosophy and the brain sciences, such as neuroethics, philosophy of neuroscience, representation in the brain, or philosophical and scientific theories of consciousness.

nodes.title: Animal Minds
groups: Concentration I - Core Philosophy: D.
Concentration II - Ethics and Public Policy: E.
nodes.prereq_text: Philosophy 100D, or two prior courses in philosophy.
nodes.description: The goal of this course is to examine current research in animal cognition with a view to understanding how philosophical and scientific questions about animal minds interact. Topics may include whether nonhuman animals can feel pain; whether they can suffer; whether they have episodic memory; whether they are conscious. We will also consider ethical implications of the answers we find to the above questions.

nodes.title: Social Philosophy
groups: Concentration I - Core Philosophy: D.
Concentration II - Ethics and Public Policy: D.
Concentration II - Ethics and Public Policy: E.
nodes.prereq_text: Philosophy 100A; or, two prior courses in philosophy.
nodes.description: This course will examine moral problems associated with economic activity; for example, economic justice and the moral basis of property rights.

nodes.title: Philosophy of Gender
groups: Concentration I - Core Philosophy: D.
Concentration II - Ethics and Public Policy: E.
nodes.prereq_text: One course from PHIL 100A-F and one additional course in Philosophy.
nodes.description: Philosophical issues involving the concept of gender. Topics may include the distinction between sex and gender, gender and sexuality, theories of gender, gender identity and expression, non-binary and queer genders, and gender subordination and oppression.

nodes.title: Feminist Philosophy
groups: Concentration I - Core Philosophy: D.
Concentration II - Ethics and Public Policy: D.
Concentration II - Ethics and Public Policy: E.
nodes.prereq_text: Philosophy 100A; or, two prior courses in philosophy.
nodes.description: In this course, we examine philosophical approaches to feminism and feminist issues. Topics covered may include inequality in the workplace and in family structures; global feminism; objectification; pornography; and prostitution.

groups: Concentration II - Ethics and Public Policy: D.

nodes.title: Freedom and Determinism
groups: Concentration I - Core Philosophy: D.
Concentration II - Ethics and Public Policy: D.
Concentration II - Ethics and Public Policy: E.
nodes.prereq_text: Prerequisite: one prior course in philosophy.
nodes.description: Determinism is the doctrine that the laws of nature plus the past necessitate the future. Is determinism compatible with the view that we often act freely and are often morally responsible for what we do?

nodes.title: Advanced Topics in Applied Ethics.
groups: Concentration I - Core Philosophy: D.
Concentration II - Ethics and Public Policy: D.
Concentration II - Ethics and Public Policy: E.
nodes.prereq_text: Philosophy 100A; or, two prior courses in philosophy.
nodes.description: Advanced topics in applied ethics, such as the ethics of war; the ethics of procreation; and the ethics of how we treat animals.

Concentration II - Ethics and Public Policy: D.
Concentration II - Ethics and Public Policy: E.
nodes.prereq_text: Philosophy 4 or 100A; and, Philosophy 100B or 100C or 100D or 100E.
nodes.description: An examination of the nature of desires, emotions, the imagination and other aspects of human psychology, and of the ways these bear on the moral evaluation of people and actions.

nodes.title: Contemporary Philosophy
groups: Concentration I - Core Philosophy: D.
Concentration II - Ethics and Public Policy: E.
nodes.prereq_text: Philosophy 100B or 100D or 100E.

Concentration II - Ethics and Public Policy: D.
Concentration II - Ethics and Public Policy: E.

Content will vary but may include contemporary debates, such as gender, pornography, consent, single authors such as Wollstonecraft, or de Beauvoir, and themes, such as early feminist thinkers, or feminist epistemology.

nodes.title: Philosophy of Law
groups: Concentration I - Core Philosophy: D.
Concentration II - Ethics and Public Policy: D.
Concentration II - Ethics and Public Policy: E.
nodes.description: An introduction to some of the main issues generated by the philosophical question, "What is law?" In what sense is conduct made obligatory by the existence of law? What, if any, is the relationship between law and morals? What are rules? What does it mean to say that a rule exists? Do courts really apply rules or merely pretend to do so?

Concentration II - Ethics and Public Policy: D.
